speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: On top of these recommendations, the Ministry of Law (MinLaw) also conducted further studies and received extensive stakeholder feedback proposing other reforms.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In view of the large number of complex legislative changes required to give effect to the recommendations and other reforms, a phased approach to implementation was adopted.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Prior to this Bill, in 2015, the Bankruptcy Act was amended to create a more rehabilitative discharge framework for bankrupts, encourage institutional creditors to exercise financial prudence when granting credit, and facilitate better utilisation of public resources by requiring institutional creditors to appoint private trustees in bankruptcy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In 2017, the Companies Act was amended to enhance our corporate rescue and debt restructuring processes to strengthen Singapore as a forum of choice for debt restructuring.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The reforms introduced features adapted from Chapter 11 of the United States (US) Bankruptcy Code, and the United Nations Commission on International Trade Law (UNCITRAL) Model Law on Cross-Border Insolvency.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: I am pleased to report that the amendments to the Companies Act that came into effect on 23 May 2017 have made a positive impact.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: It is heartening that parties are taking advantage of the new provisions to seek better outcomes for creditors, debtors and other stakeholders, like the employees of financially distressed companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This Bill is the last phase of this current round of reforms, and builds on the foundation laid by the earlier amendments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Taken together, these reforms ensure that our insolvency and restructuring laws remain progressive and modern.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This Bill achieves this aim through three specific objectives.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: First, to promulgate a new single Act, which consolidates the corporate and personal insolvency and debt restructuring laws into one place.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: They are currently found in two separate statutes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This has numerous benefits, including setting out common principles and aligning procedures across the regimes under a single law, rationalising existing inconsistencies and minimising current uncertainty due to cross-referencing across the various pieces of legislation, and enhancing the clarity and accessibility of the laws for advisers and the parties involved.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This will be welcomed as it removes the need to refer to multiple primary and subsidiary legislation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Second, the Bill establishes a regulatory regime for insolvency practitioners.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This will professionalise and raise the quality and standards of insolvency practitioners.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Third, the Bill also enhances our insolvency and debt restructuring regimes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In particular, the reforms continue the enhancement of Singapore's corporate rescue and debt restructuring framework that commenced under the Companies Act amendments last year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The latter introduced US Chapter 11 concepts into our English law-based schemes of arrangement regime, such as worldwide moratoriums, super-priority rescue financing, prepackaged restructurings and cram-downs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This Bill will further enhance the restructuring regime, with new provisions, such as a restriction on ipso facto clauses, which I will touch on in a minute.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Taken as a whole, these reforms benefit local businesses experiencing financial difficulties by providing them with more robust tools to rehabilitate, to get back onto their feet; position Singapore as a forum of choice for foreign debtors to restructure, creating new and greater opportunities for our professional services, such as the legal, accounting and financial services; create value for our economy, by supporting Singapore’s position as an international legal, financial and business centre through a strong restructuring regime.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: With that, Mr Speaker, let me now take Members through the key provisions of the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Bill introduces a new legislation that consolidates the personal and corporate insolvency and debt restructuring laws that are currently in the Bankruptcy Act and in the Companies Act into a single Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The repeals, however, will not affect existing cases and pending applications that are now before the Courts under the current Bankruptcy Act and Companies Act, as long as they are before the date of commencement of the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The relevant provisions of the Bankruptcy Act and Companies Act will continue to apply to those cases and applications.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: I will go over some of the key provisions relating to personal bankruptcy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Clauses 273 to 437 relate to personal bankruptcy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: These provisions have been ported over from the existing provisions in the Bankruptcy Act and remain largely unchanged.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Given the significant amendments that were made in 2015, the present amendments are less substantial.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Of these, one of the changes is to make the administration of bankruptcy cases more efficient.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Currently, secured creditors do not need to indicate an intention to claim interest on debts owed by the bankrupt.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Under clause 327(4) of the Bill, secured creditors are required to notify the trustee administering the bankruptcy, within 30 days after the bankruptcy order, if they intend to claim interest on the debt for the period after the making of the order.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Given that secured creditors are in most cases paid out fully from their security, this change allows the trustee to have a more complete picture of the full extent of the bankrupt’s assets and liabilities early on.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This facilitates greater certainty and transparency in projected returns to the relevant stakeholders and also facilitates a more efficient administration of the bankruptcy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Next, I turn to liquidation which appears in clauses 119 to 250.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: These provisions have also been ported over from the Companies Act with various amendments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The key changes include the reforms made to the appointment of the Official Receiver as liquidator, the introduction of a new early dissolution procedure, and also a new wrongful trading provision.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Clause 135 sets out the circumstances where the Official Receiver may be nominated as liquidator in a Court application to wind up a company.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Currently, the Official Receiver is the default liquidator where there is no liquidator appointed by the Court, or there is a vacancy in the position of liquidator in a Court-ordered winding up.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This is undesirable because there is no obligation imposed on the applicant to attempt to appoint a private liquidator, even where the company may have sufficient assets to pay for such liquidators.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This amendment thus refocuses the Official Receiver’s role on overseeing the conduct of liquidation and cases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Under clause 135(3) of the Bill, the Official Receiver may only be nominated to act as liquidator if the applicant for a winding up has taken reasonable steps but is unable to obtain the consent of a licensed insolvency practitioner to be appointed as liquidator, and the Official Receiver then consents to such nomination.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Second, clauses 209 to 211 introduce a new procedure for the early dissolution of a company in liquidation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In the present regime, there is no summary procedure that caters to cases where companies may have insufficient assets to pay for the administration of their own winding up.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Without the new provision, a significant number of man-hours and public resources will need to be expended to liquidate such companies, with little or even no return to creditors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The early dissolution procedure may be utilised by the Official Receiver and by private liquidators who have obtained the prior consent of the Official Receiver.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: It may be used where the liquidator has reasonable cause to believe that (a) the realisable assets of the company are insufficient to pay even for the expenses of the winding up; and (b) where the affairs of the company do not otherwise require further investigation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In such cases, the liquidator may give notice to the creditors and contributories that the name of the company will be struck off the register and the company will be dissolved at the expiration of 30 days from the date of the notice.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Relevant stakeholders who oppose the early dissolution may appoint a replacement liquidator or apply to the Court for relief.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: So, there is the option if one does not agree with the proposal.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The current regime is unsatisfactory as criminal liability must first be found as a prerequisite before the making of an application to impose civil liability against the officer of the company, and has not, as far as we are aware, been used in any reported case in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Clause 239(10) further provides that a company or any person party to, or interested in becoming a party to, the carrying on of business with a company, may apply to the Court for a declaration that a particular course of conduct, transaction or series of transactions would not constitute wrongful trading.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: I now turn to deal with the licensing and regulatory regime.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Clauses 47 to 60 establishes a new licensing and regulatory regime applicable to all persons acting as “insolvency practitioners”, as defined in clause 47.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Currently, such practitioners are regulated, if at all, under the professional regimes to which they belong.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: For example, public accountants are regulated by the Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority (ACRA).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: However, there is no specific regime applicable only to and for insolvency practitioners.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This has led, in some cases, to undesirable situations where either a liquidator or a judicial manager whose conduct has fallen short of standards could not otherwise be punished besides or beyond looking at that individual’s professional licensing regime.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Its key features include: first, the licensing of insolvency practitioners, who must meet minimum qualifications and prescribed requirements to obtain and renew their licences under clauses 50 to 51.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In particular, clause 50 provides that a “qualified person” means any person who is an advocate or solicitor, a public accountant, a chartered accountant or possesses such other qualifications as the Minister may prescribe; and second, the investigation and discipline against insolvency practitioners for breaches of their conduct as insolvency practitioners under clauses 56 to 60.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: I turn next to touch on the enhancements made to our debt restructuring regime.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: A successful debt restructuring avoids liquidation and allows the company to get back onto its feet, to continue its business as a going concern.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Compared to liquidation, this provides a better return to creditors, and also benefits stakeholders, such as employees who get to keep their jobs, and trading counterparties who rely on the company's businesses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: When the Companies Act was amended last year to strengthen Singapore’s debt restructuring regime, it was noted during the Second Reading that, “ he need for debt restructuring is on the rise globally”, referring to high profile cases, such as Hanjin Shipping, and Singapore-listed businesses like Swiber and Ezra.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Since the passage of those amendments, several more high-profile cases, illustrating the need for an effective debt restructuring and rehabilitation scheme, have been in the news, including well-known names like Toys "R" Us in the US, Noble, our own Hyflux and Nam Cheong.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This Bill further strengthens our debt restructuring regimes for the rehabilitation of companies in financial distress, while including appropriate safeguards to balance the interests of stakeholders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: With this in mind, I will touch on the amendments to schemes of arrangement first, followed by judicial management and, finally, the new restrictions on ipso facto provisions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In respect of schemes of arrangement, the Bill makes two amendments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: First, clause 64 re-enacts section 211B of the Companies Act, with a new subsection (12)(b).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Clause 64(1) gives the Court the power to make one or more orders restraining certain actions and proceedings against the company on an application by a company that has proposed a compromise or arrangement with its creditors or intends to do so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Clause 64(8) provides for an automatic moratorium of not more than 30 days to apply upon the making of an application under clause 64(1).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The new clause 64(12)(b) provides that neither an order made by the Court under clause 64(1) nor the automatic moratorium under clause 64(8) affects "the commencement or continuation of any proceedings that may be prescribed by regulations." This amendment empowers the Minister to prescribe by regulations that the commencement of specified proceedings, or the continuation of specified proceedings, or both, is not affected by the moratoria.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The intention is to apply this power in a targeted manner where necessary, in particular, with respect to writs for an action in rem against a vessel.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The current practice, as I understand it, is that for urgent cases in rem, writs and applications for leave are to be filed simultaneously, and the Supreme Court registry accepts such filings with the Court thereafter deciding if the claim may proceed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The power under clause 64(12)(b) will be used to provide that the first step of the filing of an in rem writ is not itself impeded by the moratoria, and this is in order to preserve the claims against the vessels because time stops running when you have filed the claim.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: However, leave of Court under clause 64(1)(c) or (8)(c) will still be required to continue with such proceedings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: A similar provision is also inserted at clauses 65(7)(b), 95(3)(b) and 96(5)(b).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This re-enacts section 211H of the Companies Act, but with one key difference at clause 70(4)(b)(ii)(B), that persons subordinate in priority to the dissenting class must not receive or retain any property “of the company”.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: So, the insertion of the words "of the company” clarifies and confirms the position outlined in Parliament last year when this provision was introduced in the 2017 amendments, that the cram-down provisions introduced were “not concerned with adjustments to shareholder interests".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Currently, a company may only enter judicial management by a Court order.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Clause 94 provides an alternative mode of entry into judicial management in cases where creditors are supportive.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: It must be emphasised that once the company is placed into judicial management, the judicial management process will then continue in the same manner and under the supervision of the Court, regardless of how the judicial management was started.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: That is obvious because it is a judicial management with the Court having oversight.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Judicial managers are provided certain powers under those provisions set out in paragraph (f) to bring an action in Court to unwind prejudicial transactions and avoid acts detrimental to creditors, for example, where errant directors have entered into a transaction to transfer assets of the company to a third party for no value or no valuable consideration.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This new avenue of funding may increase the likelihood of such an action being pursued.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This will, in turn, benefit stakeholders by providing higher recoveries, if such actions are successful.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This new power is similarly provided to liquidators in clauses 144(1)(g) and 177(1)(a).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: To avoid doubt, these new provisions are only intended to provide for the assignment of proceeds from such an action brought by the judicial manager or liquidator.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This is not intended to affect other funding arrangements that are allowed under common law, such as funding for causes of action that belong to the company as its property, and funding for the investigation of potential causes of action for financially distressed companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Clause 102 re-enacts section 227I of the Companies Act, which provides that the judicial manager of a company is deemed to be the agent of the company, but in clause 102, it omits the imposition of personal liability on the judicial manager.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The present regime imposes personal liability on judicial managers for contracts entered into or adopted by the judicial managers, although the judicial manager is allowed to disclaim personal liability, and usually does so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The availability of such a disclaimer of personal liability ensures that the judicial manager is not otherwise discouraged from entering into or adopting contracts that would be beneficial to the company.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: I turn now to clause 440 which introduces a new restriction on the operation of certain types of ipso facto clauses. "Ipso facto" or, in English, "without more" clauses in contracts allow one party to terminate or modify a contract upon a specified event occurring to the other party.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In the restructuring and insolvency context, such clauses typically allow one party to terminate the contract upon the occurrence of a specified insolvency-related event affecting the other party, such as an application for a judicial management order or an application for a scheme under the Companies Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Currently, there is no restriction on the operation of ipso facto clauses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: If a company's business relies on key contracts and such contracts contain ipso facto clauses, that company will have difficulty commencing or entering into a debt-restructuring process because of the risk that counterparties would, simply by that reason alone, be able to terminate those key contracts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This new provision, therefore, facilitates the attempts of such a company to restructure by protecting its valuable commercial contracts from being terminated by reason only that the company has embarked on restructuring efforts, under certain specified circumstances.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The concept of restricting the application of ipso facto clauses is also found in the laws of jurisdictions, such as the US, Canada and Australia.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The language in clause 440, in particular, takes reference from section 34 of the Canadian Companies' Creditors Arrangement Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This restriction, if applicable, operates from the commencement of those restructuring proceedings, that means, from the commencement of the judicial management proceedings or the restructuring by schemes until their conclusion.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: At this juncture, it is necessary to make it clear that clause 440 only limits a certain specific subset of ipso facto clauses, those I have just outlined above, in other words, by reason only of the restructuring efforts of the company.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: It does not affect ipso facto clauses that are triggered on any other contractually provided grounds.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In a case of a developer and a main contractor entering into a contract for the construction of a building, where the contract contains ipso facto clauses that may be triggered either on the commencement of restructuring proceedings, or the failure to meet construction milestones, which is not untypical in such a contract.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: So, it is only by reason of the restructuring efforts set out in clause 440 alone that these ipso facto clauses are restricted.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: To balance the interests of the counterparty and other stakeholders, safeguards have also been included in clauses 440(4) and (5).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: First, certain types of contracts are exempted from this provision.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: These exemptions recognise that restricting the application of ipso facto clauses in certain categories of transactions or contracts would have a disproportionately adverse impact on markets, while balancing the efficacy of the restriction.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: These include prescribed eligible financial contracts and prescribed contracts that affect the national interest or economic interest of Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This provides an additional safeguard for relief in certain specific individual cases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In particular, it strengthens our corporate debt restructuring regimes to better support companies, creditors and other stakeholders who seek to rehabilitate local and foreign companies here, balancing the commercial interests of all concerned.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This Bill would not have been possible without the extensive consultation over the years with the industry bodies, with leading industry practitioners, academics and other stakeholders in the insolvency regime, such as the Courts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: These have been carefully considered in detail and incorporated into the Bill, where appropriate, and this makes the Bill far more robust.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This Bill is part of a wider concerted effort to enhance Singapore's debt restructuring ecosystem.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This follows from the MOU with the Seoul Bankruptcy Court in May earlier this year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: These MOUs with key commercial and insolvency jurisdictions bode well for the future and will facilitate efficient cross-border restructuring and insolvency proceedings between the Courts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: With this Bill, and our collective efforts, we will create a world-class restructuring and insolvency ecosystem in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I support the consolidation into one single piece of legislation existing separate statutes pertaining to personal and corporate insolvency laws and the laws to debt restructuring.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope this will allow a more unified approach to be taken by the Courts, the Insolvency and Public Trustee's Office and the insolvency practitioners.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While much of the provisions in this colossal omnibus Bill are taken from existing provisions in the Companies Act and the Bankruptcy Act, the Bill also introduces some new regulations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This follows the practice in some other countries, for example, the United Kingdom and Australia.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have a few questions regarding this new regulatory regime.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would also like to ask the Senior Minister of State, whether in the past, say, 10 years or so, there has been instances of misconduct by any insolvency practitioner or where any such practitioner has committed any acts which would have run afoul of the provisions under the new regulatory regime if this had been introduced earlier.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Perhaps the Senior Minister of State can elaborate on what are some of these acts or misconduct complained of.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In 2015, as part of the first phase of this process, the Bankruptcy Act was amended to create a more rehabilitative discharge framework for bankrupts.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Provisions of the existing Bankruptcy Act have now been incorporated into this Bill.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Has the Government conducted any studies to find out the reasons behind the increase?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What is the expected trend that the Government expects in the next two to three years?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How much success have we had in terms of attracting regional or international restructuring work?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With this Bill, there is now no need to extensively cross-reference the Companies Act and Bankruptcy Act to see how the latter is adapted to suit corporate insolvency.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By being located in a single statute, the law becomes clearer and much more accessible.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This allows some who are less familiar with our laws to consider utilising our debt restructuring regime.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Notwithstanding the focus is on companies – hence, the title Insolvency, Restructuring and Dissolution – the Bill also contains personal bankruptcy law.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This decision to keep the two bankruptcy laws within the same statute recognises that there are common principles in both situations.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Both involve a balancing of the myriad of interests in a situation where a debtor cannot repay his or her or its creditors.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Such concerns may include giving the bankrupt another chance, a trade creditor's own need for cash flow, and employees getting paid and keeping their jobs, as eloquently put forward by Mr Patrick Tay moments ago.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Nevertheless, the very nature of a company gives rise to separate concerns.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As a separate legal personality, its owners experience limited liability and it may be dissolved.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, there are different regimes for each kind of bankruptcy.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It seeks to govern liquidators, judicial managers, receivers or managers and those appointed to those positions in the interim.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With regard to this regime, what is the purpose of specifying 30 June as the date on which a valid licence that is not renewed would expire?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For that, see clause 53(2), especially since it seems as though the renewal for licences would all come at the same time.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Also, since it seems as though a written direction can convert a condition into a criminal offence if the condition was not complied with, what sort of conditions are envisioned that a licensing officer may specify under clause 52(2), especially those applicable to a specified licensee only?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I would be very open to hearing the Senior Minister of State's clarifications on these points.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There are also some amendments that alter contractual rights.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The first is that affecting secured creditors of personal bankrupts.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Secured creditors enjoy proprietary interest such that the security is, in the context of a company, not considered part of the company's assets.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What safeguards are there to ensure that the secured creditor's interests in having a security are not unfairly prejudiced, even as this amendment seeks to ascertain assets and liability early for a more efficient administration of the bankruptcy?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I heard the Senior Minister of State expound quite fluidly on ipso facto clauses when he first read the Second Reading speech.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Allow me to share my views on it.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Ipso facto clauses allow termination or modification of the contract upon the occurrence of a specified trigger event.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In principle, this provision is important because it ensures that the objectives of an attempted rehabilitation of the company are achieved.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It may alter risk-allocation and also may increase uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Revised Report of the Insolvency Law Reform Committee stated, "ability of the insolvent company to cherry-pick contracts would disrupt the rules on set-off and netting by making it difficult to isolate which contracts should be eligible for set-off or netting." Nevertheless, this is not something novel for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Other jurisdictions have looked into having a similar provision before, for example, my research shows the US, Canada, France and Australia.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Having said so, I seek a clarification from the good Senior Minister of State, how is clause 440 calibrated to balance between these different considerations and reduce possible negative market impact?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Moving on, Sir, regarding the proof of debts, was it intended for the law on provability of debts to change its reference point from the making of the winding up order to the making of the application for winding up?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Clause 218(2) provides that "the following are provable where a company is in judicial management or an insolvent company is being wound up: (a) any debt or liability in which the company (i) is subject at the commencement of the judicial management or winding up, as the case may be." The next paragraph also references the commencement of judicial management or winding up.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I seek the Senior Minister of State's clarification on this one.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Besides some major amendments, Sir, this Bill also continues to refine the relevant regimes.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For instance, clause 102 omits personal liability for judicial managers.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Clause 250(1) and clause 186 address issues that have arisen before our Courts.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It finally introduces the omnibus legislation covering personal and corporate insolvency laws, widely awaited by practitioners in the insolvency sphere.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As the learned Senior Minister of State mentioned, it follows two reports, the 2013 Report of the Insolvency Law Review Committee as well as the 2016 Report issued by the Committee to Strengthen Singapore as an International Centre for Debt Restructuring co-headed by the learned Minister Ms Indranee Rajah and the Hon Justice Kannan Ramesh.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There was also an earlier report, the 2002 report by the Company Legislation and Regulatory Framework Committee, which made a clarion call at the outset for the introduction of a consolidated new insolvency Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would, however, make a point that in providing for these provisions to basically enhance Singapore's status as a premier debt restructuring centre, we must also need to balance against the creditors' interest.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Tilting against the creditors, especially banks, would result in higher business cost and it being more difficult for the banks to conduct the business, particularly given the regulatory requirements that it has under Basel III to ensure better ability on their part to liquidate collateral in a timely manner.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This may, in turn, impact Singapore's attractiveness as a financial centre or, if the cost of lending goes up, then the cost will be passed on to the businesses.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As we all appreciate, the vast majority of companies in Singapore are solvent, so we must ensure that we do not have a situation of the tail wagging the dog.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We note that in 2017, a number of pieces of legislation have been passed making inroads into the rights of creditors, for example, the more extensive moratoriums, the possibility of rescue financing with the consequent super priority afforded to the rescuers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And it is in that context that I wish to seek a fuller explanation on the proposed section 440 of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My Parliamentary colleague, Mr Christopher de Souza, spoke eloquently about it a few minutes ago.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: From my sensing, there is some level of nervousness on the impact of this provision.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Take, for example, a bank or securities company that provides margin financing to a company trading in listed securities.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The bank or securities company is exposed to the stock exchange or clearing house when putting through trade transactions of a company that is distressed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The securities company has itself to place margins with the clearing house or stock exchange.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If it cannot enforce through exercise of the ipso facto clause to terminate facilities, there is a potential exposure to them.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This may affect the bank’s practice which may become more conservative in providing margin facilities and this, in turn, may have some far reaching or unintended consequences.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In an economic situation where providing liquidity becomes important to keep companies afloat, this becomes an even greater issue.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For example, in the European Union, there are the financial collateral directives.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Another potential effect would be in relation to the private wealth management business.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Would private banks rather use offshore Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs), as opposed to Singapore SPVs, because of the potential for Singapore insolvency laws applying to these offshore SPVs or, alternatively, minimise the transactions such that there would not be a substantial Singapore connection between the foreign SPVs and Singapore?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This substantial connection test is the basis upon which Singapore Courts can exercise jurisdiction over a foreign SPV.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Notwithstanding what I have said, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These are very thoughtful, considerate comments and I will do my best to respond to them.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I will do so, grouping them into five different topics.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The first relates to the consolidation of personal and corporate restructuring and insolvency laws into one single legislation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, the new licensing and regulatory regime which regulates all insolvency practitioners.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Third, the proof of debts during winding up.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Fourth, the availability of third-party funding in judicial management and liquidation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And finally, the need to safeguard the interests of creditors and employees, a point that Mr Patrick Tay spoke very passionately about.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Both Mr Murali Pillai and Mr Christopher de Souza commented on the benefits brought about by the Bill, which consolidates the personal and corporate insolvency provisions into one.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I take this opportunity to highlight that the Bill also sets out common principles that run across the different regimes, where possible.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, for example, Part 9 introduces new provisions that are generally applicable to both judicial management and winding up.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Currently, this is given effect to in judicial management and winding up by way of cross-referencing provisions in the Bankruptcy Act.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In the Bill, these regimes now have provisions specific to themselves, with the necessary refinements to ensure that they are worded in the terminology consistent with the judicial management and winding up regimes.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These include the provisions relating to proofs of debt in clauses 218 to 223, and the adjustment of prior transactions in clauses 224 to 229.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, the Bill also introduces new provisions for disclaimer of onerous property, for judicial management and winding up in clauses 230 to 233, and personal bankruptcy in clauses 373 to 376.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In particular, clauses 230(4)(a) and 373(4)(a) are new provisions that require the judicial manager, liquidator or Official Assignee, as the case may be, where the property is subject to any written law under the Second Schedule, to give notice of the intention to disclaim the property to the relevant regulatory authority.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This written notice must be given before the officeholder may give the notice of disclaimer under clauses 230(1) or 373(1).

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This ensures that the relevant regulatory authority has the opportunity to address any issues relating to the property under the relevant environmental legislation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On the new licensing and regulatory regime, a point that both Mr Dennis Tan and Mr Christopher de Souza spoke about, Mr Christopher de Souza, in particular, noted that the new requirements to act as a practitioner are more stringent than the previous ones.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is also necessary to ensure that only "fit and proper" persons who are qualified are granted such licences to allow the licensee to undertake the spectrum of restructuring and insolvency work, as described in clause 47(1).

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Dennis Tan also asked about what the conditions that might be specified are.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If Mr Dennis Tan looks at clause 50(2), it provides for certain categories of persons who are qualified to act and to administer such insolvencies.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Whilst the provisions are being developed, Mr Dennis Tan can take it from me that it will be along the same vein to ensure that the relevant expertise and proper experience befit the person to manage such restructurings and insolvencies.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked about the purpose in clause 53(2) specifying 30 June as the date on which a valid licence that is not renewed would expire, given that the renewal for licences would all come at the same time.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is the point that Mr Christopher de Souza made.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Under clause 50, a “qualified person” who is eligible to hold an insolvency practitioner’s licence means any person who is an advocate or solicitor, public accountant, chartered accountant or possesses such other qualifications as the Minister may prescribe.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is really not different from the scenario that we have today in terms of the qualifications.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Currently, the registration of a public accountant or chartered accountant is valid from 1 January to 31 December of each year, whilst the practising certificates for advocates and solicitors run on a different time scale.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They are 1 April to 31 March each year.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, the specified date of 30 June provides sufficient time for applicants for an insolvency practitioner’s licence to produce the required evidence of such registration or practising certificate.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Christopher de Souza also asked, and I think he said: "  a written direction can convert a condition into a criminal offence if the condition is not complied with, what kind of conditions are envisaged that a licensing officer may specify under clause 52(2)?” Let me clarify.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, one is a criminal offence which Mr Christopher de Souza has in mind and the other is a regulatory breach.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Such written direction may require the licensee to comply with, or cease the contravention of, any provision of Part 3 Division 3 or any condition of the licence, or make good any default arising from the contravention, or both.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, regarding the type of conditions that is envisaged to be specified, one example would be for the practitioner to comply with all the relevant statutory requirements under the Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: MinLaw will take reference from other professional licensing regimes when formulating the licensing conditions, a point in response to Mr Dennis Tan's query.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked, in the context of a winding up, if it is intended for clause 218 on provability of debts to change its reference point from the making of the winding up order to the making of the application for the winding up.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In the case of a winding up pursuant to a Court order, the reference point is the making of the winding up order itself.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Christopher de Souza also referred to clause 218(2)(a)(i) and (ii), where the phrase "commencement of the judicial management or winding up" is used.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: A similar phrase "commencement of the winding up" is also used at clause 218(1)(a)(i) and (ii).

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And the meaning of those phrases must be ascertained in the context of the provision itself.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In other words, the phrase used in this clause is not defined in Part 9 and, considering the context of this clause in the manner described above, the plain and ordinary meaning of these words would apply.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These are for the words the "commencement of the judicial management”, it means the time when the appointment of a judicial manager takes place.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And the words the "commencement of the winding up” means the time when the winding up order is made or the passing of the resolution for a voluntary winding up, if it is done out of Court.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Where the phrase is intended to bear a technical meaning, other than the plain and ordinary meaning, a separate definition is used to provide for that technical meaning.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In the context of clauses 224 to 229, where it is intended for a technical meaning to apply, clause 217(1) sets out the definition for that technical meaning, which applies only for the purposes of clauses 224 to 229.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Further, Mr Christopher de Souza also asked if the technical meaning of "commencement of winding up” in clause 126 applies to clause 218.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Clause 126 in Part 8 Division 2 applies to applicable provisions in that Division, such as clause 130, which requires the technical meaning provided under clause 126.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The technical meaning in clause 126 does not apply to clause 218, which is in Part 9.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I turn now to Mr Murali Pillai's comment about how the Bill enhances the availability of third-party funding that allows the judicial manager or liquidator to pursue claims against parties on behalf of the company.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I earlier mentioned the new option which allows the judicial manager or liquidator to assign proceeds from an action set out in those provisions to a third-party, in exchange for funding of the action.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Where the company is in winding up, I would like to point out an enhancement to an existing option for funding by creditors under section 328(10) of the Companies Act, which is re-enacted with modification at clause 204, and it is as follows.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Currently, the main drawback of section 328(10), as Mr Murali Pillai might be aware, was as stated by the Insolvency Law Review Committee and I quote, "the Court may make an order only after the relevant assets have been recovered, protected or preserved, or after the relevant expenses have been recovered.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: At the point of providing the funds or the indemnity, the funding creditors at that stage will have no assurance that the Court will make an order giving them an advantage over other creditors in consideration." That is a limitation to the current regime in section 328(10) of the Companies Act.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Next, various Members spoke up about safeguarding the interests of creditors and I will turn to this point now.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Murali Pillai, in particular, commented that there is a need to balance the interests of creditors against those of companies, and I agree entirely.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Specifically, in relation to Mr Murali Pillai's query on how the balance between a financial centre and being an international centre for debt restructuring should be struck, I should say that these two objectives are not mutually exclusive.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In fact, in many ways, they are complementary.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We want businesses to be set up here, thrive, function and operate.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But when they fall into difficult times, given the impact it has on various stakeholders, in terms of the creditors, employees and other counterparties, we want to provide them with the best possible tools and the best regime possible in this forum to restructure and get back on their feet.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It enhances our capabilities to provide a comprehensive end-to-end suite of options for businesses and transactions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I turn now to the ipso facto clauses which several Members spoke on, on clause 440.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Both Mr Christopher de Souza and Mr Murali Pillai commented on the potential consequences of clause 440 in exposing creditors to greater risk and uncertainty and have asked how it is calibrated to address these consequences and balance the different considerations.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To start, let me reiterate the reasons for introducing the restriction.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: He has read both of the committees' reports.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Both committees obviously had the ipso facto provision before it but, at that stage, chose not to recommend it as being as one of the options.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In other words, solely when a company applies to Court, or voluntarily takes a restructuring step, it is in that limited scenario that the ipso facto clauses are being sought to be restricted.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Such actions undermine the prospects of achieving a successful restructuring.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As Mr Christopher de Souza has pointed out, having this restriction will give the company necessary time and room to restructure, by protecting the company's valuable commercial contracts from termination or modification.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In other words, if one is about to restructure and get the company back onto its feet, the last thing it wants is for valuable counterparty contracts to be terminated for no reason other than that it has now sought protection from the Courts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These restrictions allow a company to continue with the key commercial contracts to generate revenue, or which enable the company to continue operations itself and thus preserving and enhancing the value of the company itself.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Take the example of Hyflux, a recent case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Shortly after filing for a moratorium under the current regime to support its restructuring proceedings, certain creditors declared an event of default had occurred because of the moratorium filing.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, no other breach of that underlying provision, but because of Hyflux's filing of the moratorium protection and the application to Court to protect and enhance its restructuring efforts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Based on this event of default, the creditors exercised their contractual rights, such as the acceleration of repayment terms and set-off rights in respect of debts owing by the creditor to Hyflux.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, the moment that happened, some creditors, exercising contractual rights under the ipso facto provisions, provided for accelerated repayments to be made when it was otherwise not yet due or provided for set-off rights that they could not exercise immediately.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, all of these steps diminish and restrict Hyflux's cash flow.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And that is not an untypical situation that happens.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And this thereby further exacerbated the financial position of the company.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Now, if a similar situation arises in the future, clause 440 would restrict creditors from exercising such rights solely on the basis of the filing of a restructuring moratorium.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This would allow the company to continue with its business operations while restructuring its debts, provided there are no other events of defaults which are triggered outside the scope of clause 440.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As Mr Murali Pillai noted, a successful restructuring benefits its creditors, as it preserves the ongoing value of a company.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I would go beyond that to say that a successful restructuring will, in fact, maximise the benefits to the company's stakeholders as a whole, including, as Mr Patrick Tay knows, its employees and also its trading counterparties.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Although the Insolvency Law Review Committee had not recommended at that time restricting ipso facto clauses in its report – this was about five years ago – this amendment is now being introduced because of further industry feedback which continued after both Committees had completed their work.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The feedback received would be that such restriction, on balance, would be beneficial to a company's rehabilitation efforts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Having said that, my Ministry is mindful that the restriction on the operation of such clauses must also balance the interests of all stakeholders, including the counterparties.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And what has been done is to calibrate clause 440 as well to introduce the ability to deal with different considerations, and I wish to just highlight and reiterate the following notable features.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It does not seek to terminate or extinguish the other party's contractual rights.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, there is no change in the rights altogether.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is only suspended during a period of time.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, the scope of this restriction is limited.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The creditors may still exercise their rights where there is another contractual ground to terminate the contract.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, in the example that Mr Murali Pillai spoke about, the securities company would be entitled to terminate the margin facilities where the company has failed to maintain sufficient collateral with the securities company, if this is otherwise a contractually provided for ground for termination.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Third, clause 440(5) provides that the restriction does not apply in respect of any legal rights under the types of contracts set out in that paragraph.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These exemptions reflect the fact that there are situations where the restriction of such clauses may have a disproportionately adverse impact on markets and also introduce uncertainty into markets which depend on established systems and norms.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Murali Pillai did speak on certain classes of financial contracts that would be eligible for such an exemption and the scope of the exemption.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will work with the relevant stakeholders to ensure that the prescribed exemptions will strike the appropriate balance amongst the interests of stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The exemptions will be finalised after we have obtained and studied feedback from stakeholders as well as the experience in other jurisdictions which have introduced the ipso facto restrictions ahead of us.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To the extent that certain contracts will fall within the exemption as an "eligible financial contract", this will ameliorate any potential negative impact on the industries that rely on such contracts for various commercial reasons.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This includes, no doubt, the wealth management industry that Mr Murali Pillai spoke about, which is also an industry that we will consider as we take feedback on what would constitute an eligible financial contract.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This builds in a degree of flexibility, depending on the impact that it may have in a particular situation or on a particular creditor.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And this can be determined by the Court on the basis of facts and context in that case and on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As highlighted above, whilst the Bill facilitates the rehabilitation of distressed companies, we have taken efforts to ensure that the overall regime does strike a sufficient balance to ensure that the interests of all stakeholders in this ecosystem are fair and balanced.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Moving forward, we will continue to study developments, both locally and also abroad, so as to ensure that the regime continues to balance the interests of all stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Christopher de Souza expressed some concern that such a requirement might be prejudicial to a secured creditor’s interest and asked if there are safeguards in place.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, it is for a period of time post the making of the bankruptcy order.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To avoid doubt, this does not in any way affect the secured creditor’s security interest.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The intention of this change is, as Mr Christopher de Souza mentioned, to facilitate a more efficient administration of the bankruptcy by ensuring all stakeholders, including the Official Assignee, are on the same page with respect to the bankrupt’s total liabilities and, consequently, the value of the assets in the bankrupt’s estate that would be available for distribution.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In addition, the subsidiary legislation under the Bankruptcy Act currently requires a bankruptcy order to be gazetted and advertised no later than 21 days after the bankruptcy order is made.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: A notice requirement will likely be re-enacted in the subsidiary legislation under this Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These requirements ensure that sufficient notice is provided to all stakeholders, including secured creditors.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Secured creditors would thus be notified of a bankruptcy order and, in turn, allow the secured creditor to notify the Official Assignee of the intention to claim interest under clause 327(4).

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I now want to move on to Mr Patrick Tay's points, his very passionate points, on the interests of the employees, a point that Mr Tay has raised several times and I would like to turn to those points now.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Essentially, Mr Patrick Tay's points focus on the need to protect the employees' claims for unpaid salaries in the context of insolvency and Mr Tay touched on this issue in two different scenarios.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The first, where the company is in a restructuring proceeding and, second, where the company is in a liquidation proceeding and the difference between those two is obviously that, in a liquidation scenario, it is terminal, there is one outcome.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The approach and treatment of such claims under those situations are different consequently, with good reasons for this.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In a restructuring situation, such as in a judicial management, the impetus is to facilitate the company restructuring its debts and, hopefully, rehabilitate its business to its former position or better.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For there to be a meaningful rehabilitation, employees are an important group of stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As Mr Patrick Tay mentioned, and I agree, "workers are the lifeblood of the company…  n times of difficulty, the company stands little chance of rehabilitation without its workers".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This will rank second in the order of priority, behind only any super-priority debt arising from rescue financing obtained pursuant to an order under clause 101(1)(b).

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Such super-priority rescue financing is integral and fundamental in most corporate restructuring cases.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: New money and injection of new capital is really the lifeblood of a successful restructuring.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And without the injection of rescue financing to aid the company during the restructuring process, the restructuring may not get off the ground.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Therefore, any potential prejudice to employees, which Mr Patrick Tay mentioned, must be balanced against the benefits of a successful restructuring, such as the potential continuation of employment and higher rate of repayment of outstanding wages, as compared to a scenario where the company goes into liquidation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Patrick Tay mentioned the grant of super-priority rescue financing cases under clauses 67 and 101 and whether they are subject to safeguards.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And, in particular, Mr Patrick Tay mentioned the case of Re Attilan Group Limited, a 2017 decision of the High Court.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Courts would, generally, be slow to allow super-priority financing unless it is strictly necessary.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That said, as I mentioned, given that new monies and new injection of capital and, in some cases, super-priority funding, in the appropriate circumstances, it will be allowed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I turn now to a scenario where employees' wages are not paid in an insolvent liquidation scenario.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As I mentioned earlier, this procedure is terminal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It leads to the dissolution of the company and it is so because there are insufficient assets to meet the myriad competing creditors’ claims.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In this context, the order of priority provided under clause 203 strikes the appropriate balance in according such priority, taking into consideration the nature of the varying claims against the company.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The costs and expenses of liquidation and the expenses of the applicant for the winding up order are paid out first under clause 203(1)(a) to (c) before any of the other preferential debts under clause 203(1), a point that Mr Patrick Tay mentioned earlier.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Removing the priority for these categories of claims would deter insolvency practitioners from undertaking liquidations because they would have little assurance of recovering the costs and expenses of such liquidations.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This would severely undermine an orderly liquidation and distribution of dividends, to the detriment of all stakeholders, including employees.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, we are dealing with the costs and expenses of undertaking the liquidation in the first place.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Patrick Tay then mentioned that because of the provisions, what used to be ranked No 2 for the employees' claims is now ranked No 4.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This clearly and unequivocally affirms the importance of employees by providing such debts priority over all other lower-ranked preferential debts and all other unsecured debts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Patrick Tay mentioned that whereas currently employees’ wages are ranked second under section 328(1)(b) of the Companies Act, clause 203(1)(d), however, provides that unpaid wages are ranked fourth amongst preferential debts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is because the debts mentioned under the new clause 203(1)(a) to (c) are currently placed together under section 328(1)(a) of the Companies Act.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, in other words, what went into section 328(1)(a) of the Companies Act would be clause 203(a), (b) and (c).

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Lastly, Mr Patrick Tay asked for some statistics.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They are not available, but I thank Mr Patrick Tay and also Mr Dennis Tan for raising some suggestions on the avenues.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Patrick Tay also talked about having MOM make those claims first and then to stand in queue.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is probably better addressed to MOM because it is a burden you are asking them to take on and then wait in queue for the claims.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But Mr Patrick Tay has our assurance that the structure of the preferential payments will continue to place the employees high up on the scale and behind really only the provisions that deal with expenses of the liquidation so that we can be assured that the liquidation will be properly proceeded with.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I want to deal with a couple of points raised by Mr Dennis Tan.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Dennis Tan asked me about the rehabilitative framework, the Differentiated Discharge Framework (DDF).

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The scheme came into force on 1 August 2016.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: At present, it is still somewhat early to comment on the impact of the scheme because bankrupts whose bankruptcies commenced after the amendments came into force will only begin to be eligible for discharge in 2019.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To date, we have not commenced any studies on whether the DDF objectives have been met or otherwise as the scheme, given what I had said earlier, is still new.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But I thank Mr Dennis Tan for that suggestion and certainly we will look into studying the impact of DDF at the appropriate time when more data becomes available and there is a greater runway after the implementation itself.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think Mr Dennis Tan also asked about what has been the type of typical misconduct cases in the past 10 years or so.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Typically, when you have and when you appoint an insolvency practitioner, you are looking for the level of professionalism that is commensurate with what you might see from an advocate and solicitor, chartered accountant or a public accountant.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, those are the criteria we have set out.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And as I said earlier, the prescribing criteria will largely follow the same lines.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On the types of misconduct in cases, we have looked up some.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think Mr Dennis Tan might be familiar with some because they had been reported.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Not that having the new licensing regime or having a set of rules would necessarily mean that there will be no fraud, but what we want to do is to ensure that the bar or the barrier is higher so that there will be proper regulation just for insolvency practitioners and that we avoid the type of conflicts that we see, as in Mr Ewe's case, which may well be an extreme example.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But we also want to ensure that other professional misconduct-type cases like acting in conflict of interest or having unnecessarily high remuneration can be something that will be controlled.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To recap, in 2015, significant amendments were made to the Bankruptcy Act, including the introduction of the DDF, which gave bankrupts a clear target to work towards in order to be eligible for discharge.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This promoted a more rehabilitative regime where bankrupts would be given a chance to start over again.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Changes were also made to require institutional creditors to appoint private trustees in bankruptcy when making a bankruptcy application.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This change encouraged greater engagement by such creditors in the insolvency process and drives such creditors to exercise greater financial prudence when granting credit.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In 2017, the amendments to the Companies Act introduced new features to strengthen the schemes of arrangement and judicial management regimes.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This put in place a bespoke debt restructuring regime that incorporated the best features of the world’s leading regimes and these features included, one, super-priority for rescue financing in schemes of arrangement and judicial management, to encourage injection of fresh funds to assist the debtor through the restructuring processes; two, enhanced moratoriums in schemes of arrangement to provide breathing room to the debtor that is seeking a compromise or arrangement with its creditors; three, pre-packaged schemes of arrangement to fast-track pre-negotiated restructuring plans; and four, cram-down provisions that prevent a minority class of creditors from preventing a restructuring which has otherwise the support of the majority of its creditors.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Dennis Tan asked for an indication of how successful this has been.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have put the tools in place for this to be successful as an international restructuring regime.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And, finally, Members also heard me say that the Supreme Court has also signed up with the US courts on two MOUs which would cement their relationship and also take the platform on which such cases can appear or be heard in Singapore that much further.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This Bill is the culmination of the concerted efforts undertaken by the Government and other stakeholders in the insolvency ecosystem to transform and modernise our insolvency regime.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And that is with the view to cementing Singapore's position as a forum of choice for debt restructuring.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Bill also harmonises the different provisions from the Bankruptcy Act and the Companies Act, including the earlier amendments that have been made, into a single statute.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Bill contains reforms, such as the introduction of a new licensing and regulatory regime and amendments which further strengthen our debt restructuring regime, such as the introduction of judicial management by resolution of creditors and a new restriction on the operation of ipso facto clauses.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These modern and progressive reforms signal our ambition to become an international centre for debt restructuring.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have achieved quite remarkable progress on the various legislative reforms on this topic over the past three years or so.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: My Ministry will continue to work and ensure that the legal regime remains balanced, robust and, perhaps most importantly, responsive to the needs of the stakeholders in the system, be it debtors, creditors or other stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I would add in closing that all of this has really only been possible because of the efforts of all the stakeholders, all the people we have consulted, the feedback we have received.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, we are here today largely because of what we have been told, and the efforts of all the interested parties in making this happen.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We look forward to maintaining and extending those existing partnerships and fostering new collaborations as we continue to build on bold and exciting developments.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I conclude by thanking the Members for their suggestions.
